feedback.subject: Feedback on the Example Shop website review

findings.title: Your pages are slow to show their main content

severity.basis: The sampled pages were slower than the audit's slow-load threshold, and speed affects every page a visitor opens.

effort.basis: Needs a waterfall analysis first; fixes are usually theme, image and script changes rather than a rebuild.

observed.text: In our test load, the main content took between 2.6 and 3.4 seconds to appear across the 3 pages we sampled.
observed.label: LAB

observed.text: The layout also jumped around while loading; the worst shift score was 0.12.
observed.label: LAB

implications.text: Visitors who wait for a page to settle are more likely to leave before reading the offer, and the delay affects every service page the same way.
implications.label: INFER
implications.basis: General web-performance practice. No analytics data was supplied, so the size of the effect on this business is not demonstrated.

findings.caveat: Measured in one lab load on one computer through the capture proxy. Confirm with real-visitor (field) data before committing budget.
fix: Pull real-visitor speed data (Search Console, CrUX) so the starting point is not a single lab run.
Run a waterfall on the homepage to find the largest element and what delays it.
Defer or remove scripts that load before the visitor does anything.
findings.verify: Recapture. Lab load times on the sampled pages drop and field data agrees.

findings.title: Visitors and search engines run into dead or detoured links

severity.basis: Links that lead nowhere interrupt a visitor at the moment they chose to act.

effort.basis: Usually a handful of link edits, often in one shared template.

observed.text: 1 link points to a page that returns 404 or 410.
observed.label: FETCH

observed.text: 1 link points to a URL that redirects instead of the final address.
observed.label: FETCH

implications.text: A dead link is a dead end for the visitor, and repeated redirects slow every click that passes through them.
implications.label: INFER

fix: Fix or remove each broken link on the page that contains it.
Update redirected links to point straight at the final address.
findings.verify: Recapture. The broken and redirected link counts fall to zero.

findings.title: Your search-result snippets are left to chance

severity.basis: Some pages have no title or main heading at all.

effort.basis: Copywriting plus a plugin field; no engineering.

observed.text: 2 pages have no meta description, so search engines write their own snippet.
observed.label: FETCH

observed.text: 1 page has titles long enough to be cut off in results.
observed.label: FETCH

observed.text: The same title is reused across 2 groups.
observed.label: FETCH

implications.text: The snippet is the first thing a searcher reads about you; a written one can speak to the services you want to be hired for.
implications.label: INFER

fix: Write a distinct title and description for each service page first, then the rest.
Set a canonical URL on every indexable page.
findings.verify: Recapture. The counts drop to zero for the service pages.

findings.title: Duplicate and hard-to-reach pages compete with your real content

severity.basis: Large share of the captured site, but archive and duplicate pages are rarely the pages that win business.

effort.basis: A policy decision (keep, consolidate or noindex) followed by a template or plugin setting.

observed.text: 2 pages cannot be reached by following links from the homepage.
observed.label: FETCH

implications.text: Search engines see many thin, repeated pages and have to guess which one to show, which dilutes the pages you actually want found.
implications.label: INFER
implications.basis: Standard duplicate-content reasoning. Impact on this site's rankings is not demonstrated (no search data supplied).

fix: Decide which archive and duplicate page types deserve to exist (category, tag, date, print versions).
Noindex or consolidate the rest, and stop linking to them from navigation.
findings.verify: Recapture. Orphan and near-duplicate counts fall and the remaining pages have distinct text.

findings.title: Parts of the site are hard to use with assistive technology

severity.basis: Automated checks found issues, but their reach is limited to what those rules can see.

effort.basis: Most fixes are template-level, but they touch navigation, forms and colour.

observed.text: 2 pages have images without alt text.
observed.label: FETCH

implications.text: People using screen readers or low vision settings can be unable to complete forms or find contact links, which is also a legal and reputational exposure.
implications.label: INFER
implications.basis: General accessibility practice. Automated rules cover only part of WCAG, so conformance is not assessed.

findings.caveat: Automated rules cover only part of the accessibility guidelines. A manual review is still needed before claiming conformance.
fix: Give every link, button and form field a clear accessible name.
Raise text contrast where the automated test flagged it.
Add alt text to meaningful images.
findings.verify: Recapture and re-run the automated accessibility rules on the same pages.

findings.title: Some pages send mixed signals to search engines

severity.basis: Each case may be intentional, so each needs a quick review.

effort.basis: Individual tag or setting changes per page.

observed.text: 1 page is reachable by links but missing from the sitemap.
observed.label: FETCH

implications.text: When signals disagree, search engines choose for you, and the pages you care about may not be the ones shown.
implications.label: INFER
implications.basis: Search-engine documentation describes this behaviour; the effect on this site is not demonstrated.

fix: Review each page and decide whether it should be indexed.
Make the tags, sitemap and internal links agree with that decision.
findings.verify: Recapture. The conflicting-signal counts fall to zero.

findings.title: Some content looks out of date or thin

severity.basis: Quality signals matter over time, but no single page is critical.

effort.basis: Each page needs an editorial decision.

observed.text: 1 page has very little body text.
observed.label: FETCH

implications.text: Old or thin pages can read as neglected and give visitors less reason to trust or contact you.
implications.label: INFER

fix: Review each flagged page: refresh, merge or retire it.
findings.verify: Recapture. Flagged pages show a recent date or no longer appear.

glossary.plain: How long a visitor waits before the biggest thing on the page (usually a headline or a photo) shows up. Developers call it LCP.
A single timed page load on one computer. Useful for spotting problems, but real visitors on real phones can see better or worse.
Speed measured from the devices of people who actually visited. It is the fairer measure, and it was not part of this review.
A tool on your pages that comes from another company, such as chat widgets, ad trackers or font libraries. Each one is an extra thing the page must wait for.
A link that leads to a page that no longer exists. Visitors see an error and search engines see a dead end.
A forwarding instruction: "this page moved, go over there." A few are normal; long chains slow people down.
A page that exists but that nothing else on your site links to, so visitors and search engines have no path to it.
Two or more pages that say nearly the same thing. Search engines have to guess which one to show.
The headline and two-line summary shown for your page in search results. If you do not write them, Google writes them for you.
The one official web address for a page, used when the same page can be reached several ways.
A short written description of an image. Screen readers read it aloud and search engines use it to understand the picture.
Tools such as screen readers that people with low vision or motor difficulty use to browse the web.
Search engines keeping a copy of your page so it can appear in results. A page that is not indexed cannot be found by searching.

steps.title: Welcome, this is the review of Example Shop's website
body: This walk-through explains what we found on your public website, what it means in everyday terms, and what is yours to decide.
It is a snapshot taken on one date. It is not live monitoring, and it does not include rankings, traffic or sales.
Each finding is marked so you can tell the difference between what we observed and what we think. "Observed" is something we saw. "Our view" is an opinion, and it comes with the reason behind it.
We start with the five things we would fix first. At the end you can send us your thoughts.

steps.title: Your site in a few numbers
body: These numbers set the scene. None of them is a score or a verdict on its own.

tiles.label: Pages mapped
tiles.meaning: How many pages of your site we could find and read.

tiles.label: Outside websites linked
tiles.meaning: Other websites your pages link to. Each is a place a visitor can leave to.

tiles.label: Pages nobody links to
tiles.meaning: Pages that exist but have no link path from the rest of your site.

tiles.label: Typical response time
tiles.meaning: How quickly your server typically answers a request, before the page starts to draw.

tiles.label: Individual items flagged
tiles.note: Many are one cause repeated across pages.
tiles.meaning: Individual items our checks raised. Many are one cause repeated across pages, so this is not a count of separate problems.

tiles.label: Certificate days left
tiles.meaning: Days until your site's security certificate expires. If it lapses, visitors see a warning.

steps.title: Your website as a map
body: Each dot is a page and the lines are the links between them. Drag to look around; the highlights show what each caption is about.

caption.text: We mapped 25 pages of your site and 2 outside websites it links to.
caption.label: FETCH

caption.text: 2 pages returned an error or a redirect when we asked for it.
caption.label: FETCH

caption.text: The same 25 pages, grouped by how closely they link to one another: tightly linked pages sit together and loosely linked ones drift apart.
caption.label: FETCH

caption.text: The deepest page is 2 clicks from the homepage.
caption.label: FETCH

found.label: LAB

found.text: The layout also jumped around while loading; the worst shift score was 0.12.
found.label: LAB

meaning.inPlain: When someone opens your pages, the main content takes longer to appear than it should. People tend to give up on a page that stays blank.
meaning.picture: It is like a shop with a front door that sticks: the goods are fine, but some people turn around before they get in.

ifIgnored.text: Visitors on slower connections are more likely to leave before they read your offer.
ifIgnored.basis: General web-performance practice. No analytics were supplied, so the effect on your business is not measured here.

beats.yourPart: Agree that speed is worth a short investigation, and ask your developer or host for real-visitor speed data so we start from facts and not one test.
howFixed: Pull real-visitor speed data (Search Console, CrUX) so the starting point is not a single lab run.
Run a waterfall on the homepage to find the largest element and what delays it.
Defer or remove scripts that load before the visitor does anything.
askYourTeam: Has anyone timed the site on a phone on mobile data?
Which add-on scripts could we live without?

steps.title: A sensible order of work
body: Quick, low-effort items come first. Each one has an owner, so nothing waits for someone who does not know it is theirs.

steps.title: What this review does not tell you
body: A fair reading includes the gaps. These are things this review did not measure.

claims.text: Real-visitor speed (field data) was not measured; speed figures come from a lab load.
claims.label: SCOPE

claims.text: Browser tests covered 3 sampled pages, not the whole site.
claims.label: SCOPE

claims.text: Security headers were read from the homepage response only.
claims.label: SCOPE

claims.text: Rankings, traffic and conversions are not part of this data. No search or analytics account was connected.
claims.label: SCOPE

claims.text: Automated accessibility rules cover only part of the guidelines; a manual review is still needed.
claims.label: SCOPE

steps.title: Questions to take to your team
body: You do not need to answer these now. They are the questions that will move the work forward.

steps.title: Tell us what you think
body: Your answers and any notes below are only on this device until you choose to send them.
Check the summary, add anything you like, then send it to us by email.

top.basis: Ranked by priority level first, then by how many distinct pages are affected. A site-wide issue counts as every page.

responses.note: The viewer records the recipient's checkpoint answers and comments as { reportId, answers, comments } and lets them email it to the agency. This file never contains them.
